papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression paradigm in deep learning that addresses the challenge of deploying large, computationally expensive models in resource-constrained environments. The technique operates on a teacher-student framework, where a smaller, more efficient 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This process transfers the rich, generalized knowledge from the teacher, allowing the student to achieve high accuracy with a significantly smaller computational footprint. While initially developed for creating compact and faster models, the applications of knowledge distillation have expanded significantly, proving its versatility for enhancing model performance, improving generalization, and transferring complex capabilities across various domains like natural language processing and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Technique for Model Compression and Performance Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful machine learning technique for compressing large, complex models into smaller, more efficient versions without a significant loss in performance. This process involves training a smaller 'student' model to replicate the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The core idea is to transfer the generalized knowledge learned by the teacher, which is often encoded in its output probabilities, to the student. This allows for the deployment of state-of-the-art models in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices or applications with strict latency requirements. The applications of knowledge distillation are broad, spanning natural language processing, computer vision, recommender systems, and graph-based learning. Beyond simple model compression, distillation has been shown to improve the accuracy of student models, facilitate domain adaptation, and enable training even when the original data is unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression and Performance Enhancement in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique for model compression and performance optimization in deep learning. It involves training a smaller, more efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This process transfers the rich knowledge learned by the teacher, enabling the student to achieve comparable or even superior performance with significantly fewer parameters and lower computational cost. Various strategies have been developed, including distilling knowledge from the teacher's final outputs, internal feature representations, or an ensemble of multiple teachers. This methodology has been successfully applied across a wide range of domains, including natural language processing, computer vision, speech recognition, and federated learning, to create compact, fast, and effective models suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Model Compression Technique in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique designed to create smaller, more efficient deep learning models. The process operates on a teacher-student framework, where a compact student model is trained to mimic the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. By transferring the rich knowledge from the teacher, typically through its output probabilities or internal representations, the student model can achieve comparable accuracy with significantly lower computational and memory requirements. This enables the deployment of complex, state-of-the-art models in resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices. The applications of this versatile technique are broad, extending beyond simple compression to performance enhancement and knowledge transfer across various domains, including natural language processing and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful model compression technique where a compact 'student' model learns from a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This process aims to transfer the teacher's learned knowledge, enabling the student to achieve comparable performance with significantly fewer parameters and lower computational cost. The transfer can occur through various means, including mimicking the teacher's output probabilities or its internal feature representations. Advanced methods have emerged, such as online distillation where models teach each other, and meta-learning approaches where the teacher adapts its training strategy to better instruct the student. This technique has found broad applications in both natural language processing and computer vision, enabling the deployment of sophisticated models in resource-constrained environments by creating efficient, task-specific networks for tasks ranging from language understanding to 3D object detection.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for CTR Prediction
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, deep learning-based models have been widely studied for click-through rate (CTR) prediction and lead to improved prediction accuracy in many industrial applications. However, current research focuses primarily on building complex network architectures to better capture sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The increased model complexity may slow down online inference and hinder its adoption in real-time applications. Instead, our work targets at a new model training strategy based on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning framework to transfer knowledge learned from a teacher model to a student model. The KD strategy not only allows us to simplify the student model as a vanilla DNN model but also achieves significant accuracy improvements over the state-of-the-art teacher models. The benefits thus motivate us to further explore the use of a powerful ensemble of teachers for more accurate student model training. We also propose some novel techniques to facilitate ensembled CTR prediction, including teacher gating and early stopping by distillation loss. We conduct comprehensive experiments against 12 existing models and across three industrial datasets. Both offline and online A/B testing results show the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

papers_seen.author: West
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework Beyond Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a pivotal technique in deep learning, initially conceived as a method for model compression. This process involves transferring knowledge from a large, complex "teacher" model to a smaller, more efficient "student" model, enabling the deployment of powerful neural networks in resource-constrained environments. However, the utility of knowledge distillation extends far beyond simple compression. It serves as a powerful framework for enhancing model performance, improving robustness, and increasing the interpretability of opaque "black-box" models. By leveraging the rich, nuanced information captured by teacher models, knowledge distillation can guide student models to achieve superior accuracy, sometimes even surpassing their teachers, and can transform complex neural networks into simpler, more transparent structures like decision trees. This makes it a versatile and indispensable tool in the modern deep learning and natural language processing toolkit.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prevalent model compression technique designed to transfer knowledge from a large, complex model, known as the 'teacher', to a smaller, more efficient 'student' model. The primary goal is to reduce computational and memory requirements for deployment while maintaining high performance. papers_seen.author: Jacobs

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful and flexible technique to address the challenge of deploying large, computationally expensive deep learning models. This process involves training a smaller, more efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model, effectively transferring its learned knowledge. The primary benefit is the creation of compact, fast models suitable for resource-constrained environments without a significant loss in performance. This approach has proven effective across a wide range of applications, including natural language processing and computer vision, and its utility extends beyond simple compression to areas like performance enhancement and knowledge transfer across different tasks.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Farrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning has produced increasingly large and complex models that achieve state-of-the-art performance but are often impractical for deployment due to their computational and memory requirements. Model compression techniques, particularly knowledge distillation, address this challenge by transferring knowledge from a large, cumbersome 'teacher' model to a smaller, more efficient 'student' model. This process enables the creation of compact models that retain a significant portion of the teacher's performance, making them suitable for resource-constrained environments like mobile devices. The flexibility of knowledge distillation is evident in its successful application across various domains, including natural language processing, speech recognition, and graph-based learning, as well as its adaptability to scenarios where the original training data is unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a critical technique for model compression in deep learning. This method addresses the challenge of deploying large, computationally expensive models in resource-constrained environments by training a smaller 'student' model to mimic a larger 'teacher' model. Through this teacher-student paradigm, the compact student model inherits the rich, nuanced knowledge of its teacher, enabling high performance with a significantly smaller footprint. While initially developed for creating lightweight models for devices like smartphones, the applications of knowledge distillation have expanded. It is now a versatile framework used not only for compression but also for enhancing model performance, improving generalization, and enabling knowledge transfer in various advanced learning scenarios, solidifying its role as a foundational tool in modern artificial intelligence.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Meza
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: The increasing size and computational complexity of modern deep learning models pose significant challenges for their deployment in real-world, resource-constrained environments. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful and flexible model compression technique to address this issue. It operates on a teacher-student framework, where a smaller, more efficient student model is trained to mimic the behavior and inherit the knowledge of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. This process enables the creation of compact, high-performance models suitable for devices with limited computational power or strict latency requirements. While initially developed for size reduction, the applications of this paradigm have expanded to include performance enhancement, improved model robustness, and knowledge transfer across different tasks and domains, making it a crucial tool for developing practical and powerful artificial intelligence systems.

The primary goal is to create smaller, more efficient models suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments without a significant loss in performance. This is achieved by transferring the rich knowledge embedded in the teacher's outputs or internal feature representations to the student. The applications of this versatile framework are widespread, spanning natural language processing, computer vision, and recommender systems. Beyond simply reducing model size, knowledge distillation is also used to enhance student model performance, improve generalization, and address challenges such as data privacy and algorithmic fairness.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Technique for Model Compression and Knowledge Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful model compression paradigm where a compact "student" network learns from a larger "teacher" network. This technique facilitates the deployment of complex deep learning models in settings with limited computational resources. The process involves transferring knowledge through various mechanisms, including mimicking the teacher's final outputs, aligning intermediate feature representations, or preserving relational knowledge. Knowledge distillation has been successfully applied across diverse fields such as natural language processing, computer vision, and speech recognition. Beyond simple compression, this framework can be used for more advanced purposes, including transferring specific properties like adversarial robustness or inductive biases between different model architectures. It also enables novel applications like cross-modal learning and improving models in federated learning environments.

papers_seen.author: Allison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Technique for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning models, particularly in natural language processing and computer vision, have grown increasingly large and computationally expensive. This trend presents significant challenges for deploying these models in resource-constrained environments. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful and flexible model compression technique to address this issue. It involves training a smaller, more efficient 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This process transfers the rich knowledge learned by the teacher, enabling the student to achieve performance far exceeding what it could attain by training on the data alone. The applications of this paradigm are diverse, extending beyond simple compression to areas like continual learning, data-free learning, and unifying knowledge from multiple sources.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique for model compression and performance enhancement in deep learning. It operates on a teacher-student paradigm, where a smaller, more efficient student network is trained to replicate the behavior of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. This process facilitates the creation of compact models suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices without a significant loss in performance. Methodologies have evolved beyond simply mimicking output predictions to include transferring knowledge from intermediate feature representations, employing multiple teachers, and selectively applying the teacher's knowledge. These advanced strategies have found broad applications across natural language processing and computer vision, enabling the compression of large language models, improving machine translation, and even enhancing algorithmic fairness.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Long
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a critical model compression technique in deep learning and natural language processing. The method operates on a teacher-student framework, where a smaller, more efficient 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This process facilitates the creation of compact, fast, and resource-efficient models that retain high accuracy, enabling the deployment of complex neural networks on devices with limited computational capabilities. While initially developed for model compression, the applications of knowledge distillation have expanded significantly, now encompassing performance enhancement, improved model robustness, and knowledge transfer across different tasks and domains, making it a multifaceted tool for developing practical and powerful artificial intelligence systems.

papers_seen.author: Oliver
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a critical technique in deep learning for model compression and knowledge transfer. This process involves training a smaller 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model, enabling the deployment of powerful but computationally expensive networks in resource-constrained environments such as mobile devices. The student learns from the rich, generalized information encoded in the teacher's outputs, often achieving higher performance than if trained on ground-truth labels alone. Initially conceived for creating smaller and faster models, the applications of knowledge distillation have expanded significantly. It is now a versatile framework used not only for compression but also to enhance model performance, robustness, and generalization across diverse domains like natural language processing and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique in deep learning and natural language processing. It utilizes a teacher-student framework where a smaller, more compact 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The primary objective is to transfer the rich knowledge from the complex teacher to the student, thereby reducing computational and storage requirements for deployment on resource-constrained devices without a significant loss in performance. This knowledge transfer can occur through the teacher's final predictions, intermediate feature representations, or attention mechanisms. The versatility of this approach has led to its successful application across a wide range of domains and has spurred the development of advanced methods, including multi-teacher and data-free distillation.

papers_seen.author: Bell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique in deep learning designed to transfer knowledge from a large, complex model, known as the teacher, to a smaller, more efficient student model. This versatility has established knowledge distillation as a fundamental tool for developing more practical, efficient, and capable artificial intelligence systems across various domains, including Natural Language Processing (NLP).

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Knowledge Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique in deep learning for compressing large, complex models into smaller, more efficient ones. This process involves training a compact 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a pre-trained, cumbersome 'teacher' model. The primary goal is to retain the high performance of the teacher model while significantly reducing computational and storage costs, making advanced models deployable on resource-constrained devices. Beyond simple output matching, advanced methods focus on transferring knowledge from intermediate feature representations and using adversarial techniques to improve the student's learning process. This versatility makes knowledge distillation a crucial tool for optimizing and deploying state-of-the-art neural networks in real-world scenarios.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Beyond

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework Beyond Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique in deep learning designed to create smaller, more efficient models from larger, more complex ones. Operating on a teacher-student framework, it trains a compact student model to replicate the behavior of a pre-trained teacher model, effectively transferring its learned knowledge. While the primary goal is model compression to enable the deployment of state-of-the-art models on resource-constrained devices, its utility extends significantly. The framework has evolved to enhance model performance, improve robustness, and address critical concerns such as algorithmic fairness and data privacy. papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Technique for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression paradigm where a compact "student" model learns from a larger, more complex "teacher" model. The goal is to create lightweight, efficient models suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments without a significant drop in performance. This is achieved by training the student to mimic the outputs or internal representations of the teacher, thereby transferring its learned knowledge. This technique has been successfully applied to compress massive language models like BERT into simpler architectures. The effectiveness of distillation can be further improved when combined with other methods, such as model pre-training and low-precision quantization, making it a versatile and powerful tool in deep learning.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a crucial technique for model compression in deep learning, addressing the challenge of deploying large, computationally intensive models. This paradigm operates on a teacher-student framework, where a compact student model is trained to mimic the behavior and knowledge of a larger, more powerful teacher model. By transferring the rich information learned by the teacher, typically encoded in its output probabilities or internal features, the student can achieve comparable performance with a significantly smaller size and faster inference speed. This enables the use of state-of-the-art architectures in resource-constrained environments like mobile devices. The applications of this versatile technique extend beyond simple compression to include performance enhancement, improved generalization, and knowledge transfer across diverse domains.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique used in deep learning to create smaller, more efficient models. The process involves transferring knowledge from a large "teacher" model to a more compact "student" model. This allows for the deployment of powerful artificial intelligence systems on resource-constrained devices, such as mobile phones, without a significant loss in performance. The technique is versatile, with applications across various domains including natural language processing and computer vision, and is also used to enhance model performance and address other challenges like domain adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression and Performance Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique for model compression, enabling the creation of smaller, more efficient student models by transferring knowledge from larger, cumbersome teacher models. This process allows for the deployment of state-of-the-art deep learning architectures in resource-constrained environments. Beyond simple compression, knowledge distillation has emerged as a versatile framework that can also enhance a model's generalization capabilities, improve its robustness against adversarial attacks, and increase its interpretability. By leveraging the rich information contained in a teacher's predictions, this technique offers a multifaceted approach to optimizing neural networks for a wide range of practical applications in natural language processing and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: West
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework Beyond Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a pivotal technique in deep learning, initially conceived as a method for model compression. This process involves transferring knowledge from a large, complex "teacher" model to a smaller, more efficient "student" model, enabling the deployment of powerful neural networks in resource-constrained environments. However, the utility of knowledge distillation extends far beyond simple compression. It serves as a powerful framework for enhancing model performance, improving robustness, and increasing the interpretability of opaque "black-box" models. By leveraging the rich, nuanced information captured by teacher models, knowledge distillation can guide student models to achieve superior accuracy, sometimes even surpassing their teachers, and can transform complex neural networks into simpler, more transparent structures like decision trees. This makes it a versatile and indispensable tool in the modern deep learning and natural language processing toolkit.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Lambert
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique in deep learning designed to transfer knowledge from a large, complex model, known as the 'teacher', to a smaller, more efficient 'student' model. The primary objective is to enable the deployment of powerful, state-of-the-art models on resource-constrained devices by reducing their size and computational requirements without a substantial loss in performance. The process typically involves training the student to mimic the rich output distributions of the teacher, which contain more information than simple ground-truth labels. The applications of this paradigm are extensive, spanning natural language processing and computer vision. Advanced methods have evolved to include transferring knowledge from intermediate layers, using multiple teachers, and extending the technique's utility beyond compression to areas such as improving model robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: The Expanding Role of Knowledge Distillation in Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique in deep learning where knowledge from a large, complex "teacher" model is transferred to a smaller, more efficient "student" model. Originally conceived as a method for model compression, its applications have expanded significantly. This technique not only enables the deployment of state-of-the-art models in resource-constrained environments but also serves as a mechanism to enhance the performance of student models beyond what they could achieve through standard training. The versatility of knowledge distillation is demonstrated by its application across diverse domains, from natural language processing to computer vision. Recent advancements have introduced more dynamic and effective distillation frameworks, such as online and self-distillation, and have even leveraged the technique to improve model interpretability.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile and Effective Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: The increasing size and computational complexity of state-of-the-art deep learning models pose significant challenges for their deployment in resource-constrained environments. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful model compression technique to address this issue. This method utilizes a teacher-student framework, where a smaller, more efficient student model is trained to mimic the behavior and outputs of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. By transferring the rich, generalized knowledge from the teacher, the student model can achieve comparable performance with a significantly smaller footprint. The utility of this framework extends beyond simple size reduction, proving effective for enhancing model performance, improving generalization, and even mitigating societal biases. Knowledge distillation is a critical and versatile tool for developing efficient, practical, and accessible AI systems.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular model compression technique designed to create smaller, more efficient deep learning models without significant performance loss. The process involves training a compact 'student' model to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This allows for the deployment of complex neural networks on resource-constrained devices, such as mobile phones. The transfer of knowledge can occur by replicating the teacher's output predictions, its internal representations, or by using more advanced methods like adversarial learning. This technique has been successfully applied across various domains, including natural language processing for compressing large language models, computer vision for efficient image recognition and synthesis, and even in specialized fields like medical imaging and federated learning.

papers_seen.abstract: Large-scale deep learning models often have computational and storage requirements that hinder their deployment in practical, resource-constrained environments. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a key model compression technique to overcome this challenge. It operates under a teacher-student paradigm, where a smaller, more efficient student model is trained to mimic the behavior and inherit the knowledge of a larger, pre-trained teacher model. This process enables the creation of compact, high-performance models suitable for real-world applications. The versatility of this framework extends beyond mere compression, with applications in performance enhancement, domain adaptation, and knowledge transfer in privacy-sensitive scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique in deep learning and natural language processing. It involves a teacher-student framework where a smaller, more efficient 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The primary goal is to transfer the rich knowledge from the complex teacher to the compact student, thereby reducing computational and storage requirements without a significant loss in performance. This allows for the deployment of powerful deep learning models on resource-constrained devices. The process can involve transferring knowledge from the teacher's final predictions, intermediate feature representations, or attention mechanisms, and has been successfully applied across various domains, including language modeling, machine translation, and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

The goal is to transfer the rich knowledge learned by the teacher, enabling the creation of compact models that retain high performance. This approach has proven effective across a wide range of applications, including natural language processing and computer vision, not only for creating smaller models but also for enhancing their overall performance.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Efficient Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Modern deep learning models have achieved unprecedented performance but their immense size and computational cost often hinder practical deployment. Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful model compression framework to address this challenge. It operates on a teacher-student paradigm, where a compact 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and outputs of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. This process transfers the rich, generalized knowledge from the teacher, allowing the student to achieve comparable performance with significantly fewer resources. This makes it possible to deploy state-of-the-art models on devices with limited computational power, such as mobile phones. The technique's versatility is demonstrated by its broad application across various domains, including natural language processing and computer vision, and its adaptation into advanced methods like self-distillation and data-free distillation, further expanding its utility in developing efficient and robust AI systems.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Framework for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique in deep learning that addresses the challenge of deploying large, computationally expensive models. It utilizes a teacher-student framework where a smaller, more efficient 'student' model is trained to replicate the behavior and performance of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The primary objective is to create compact models suitable for resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices, without a significant loss in accuracy. This versatile approach extends beyond simple size reduction, with applications in enhancing model performance, improving robustness and generalization, and facilitating knowledge transfer across various domains.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Framework for Model Compression and Enhancement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile model compression technique in deep learning that transfers knowledge from a large 'teacher' model to a smaller 'student' model. The primary goal is to create lightweight, efficient models suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices without a significant loss in performance. This is achieved by training the student to mimic the rich output distributions or internal representations of the teacher. Beyond model compression, this paradigm has been adapted for a wide range of applications, including enhancing model performance, improving robustness, and enabling knowledge transfer in privacy-sensitive or data-scarce scenarios. Its flexibility has made it a foundational tool in natural language processing and computer vision.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Towards Practical Lipreading with Distilled and Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Lipreading has witnessed a lot of progress due to the resurgence of neural networks. Recent works have placed emphasis on aspects such as improving performance by finding the optimal architecture or improving generalization. However, there is still a significant gap between the current methodologies and the requirements for an effective deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose a series of innovations that significantly bridge that gap: first, we raise the state-of-the-art performance by a wide margin on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively using self-distillation. Secondly, we propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, that slashes the computational cost to a fraction of the (already quite efficient) original model. Thirdly, we show that knowledge distillation is a very effective tool for recovering performance of the lightweight models. This results in a range of models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. However, our most promising lightweight models are on par with the current state-of-the-art while showing a reduction of 8.2x and 3.9x in terms of computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable the deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.

This method involves training a compact "student" model to replicate the behavior of a larger, pre-trained "teacher" model. Its primary application is to create lightweight, efficient models suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices without a significant loss in performance. The utility of knowledge distillation extends across various domains, including natural language processing for compressing large language models and computer vision for tasks like object detection and generative modeling. Advanced strategies have also been developed, such as task-adaptive compression, data-free distillation, and online learning frameworks, showcasing the versatility and ongoing evolution of this technique.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a prominent model compression technique in deep learning designed to address the challenges posed by large, computationally expensive models. This method operates on a teacher-student paradigm, where a smaller, more efficient 'student' model is trained to mimic the behavior and replicate the knowledge of a larger, pre-trained 'teacher' model. The primary goal is to create lightweight models that retain high performance while significantly reducing computational and memory requirements, making them suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments. The applications of this versatile framework are extensive, spanning domains like natural language processing and computer vision, and advanced methods have extended its utility to enhance model robustness, facilitate privacy-preserving learning, and improve generalization.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

This technique has evolved into a versatile framework for not only creating efficient models but also for enhancing model performance, improving interpretability, promoting algorithmic fairness, and enabling domain adaptation. Its flexibility and wide-ranging benefits establish knowledge distillation as a foundational tool for developing practical and robust artificial intelligence systems.
